sources.headline: Google owner Alphabet suffers its worst-ever day on stock market - as value plunges $500bn
sources.text: Shares in Google's parent company Alphabet have suffered their worst-ever day on the US stock market, falling more than 12% and knocking around half a trillion dollars off its value.

sources.headline: Live: ASX set to edge up despite $US500b Alphabet share slump overnight
sources.text: The Australian share market is likely to rise modestly on opening this morning, with ASX 200 futures up 15 points overnight.Tech giant Google and its owner, Alphabet, lost more than half a trillion US dollars amid worries AI would subsume its advertising business, the largest one-day fall in the company's history.See how the trading day unfolds on our blog.Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.PinnedFri 30 Oct 2026 at 8:11amFri 30 Oct 2026 at 8:11amMarket SnapshotBy Alison BranleyASX 200: +0.66% to 8,950 points (live numbers below)Australian dollar: -0.03% at 70.25 US centsDow Jones: -0.25% to 52,342 pointsS&P 500: -0.304% to 7,720 pointsNasdaq: -1.375% to 26,184 pointsFTSE: +0.26% to 10,722 pointsSpot gold: -0.34% to $US4,006/ounceBrent crude: $US114.88/barrelIron ore: flat at $US90.75/tonneBitcoin: -1.34% to $US77,744Prices current around 11am AEDT.Collapse all postsFilter PostsAll29Key Events3Economy2RBA2Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 11:59amFri 30 Oct 2026 at 11:59amSydney Airport strikesBy Katie SilverI gotta be specific now — people flying out of **Sydney's Kingsford Smith Airport** might experience delays today. Workers with the United Workers Union have been striking this morning and will again this evening (4:30pm–7:30pm).The union warns of delays affecting baggage, body scanning, security checkpoints and overall security monitoring at the airport. The union said the strikes are based on:Certis Security's refusal to move on their wage offer of minimum wage increases and commit to the Airport Workplace Standard.The resulting industrial action came after United Workers Union airport security members voted No to Certis's most recent pay offer.Certis Security is owned by the Singaporean global investment firm Temasek.Sydney Airport hasn't released any statements about today's strike action but warned about delays last month when workers last took industrial action against Certis. Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 11:45amFri 30 Oct 2026 at 11:45amBinance 'security issue'By Katie SilverBinance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said in a post on X there was a "security issue" and its teams were reviewing all relevant information with urgency and added that user funds were safe.It's unclear what has happened at this time — I've just reached out to the company for more information. The man synonymous with Binance, co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who no longer manages the company, wrote on X that the incident "looked like a hack".Bitcoin has dropped to six-week lows on the news, down 1%.Issuers of stablecoin Circle and Tether say they've frozen more than $2.38 billion in their stablecoin currencies on the news. Crypto firm Ripple has also reportedly frozen roughly $200 million.Binance has more than 335 million registered global users, according to its website. Any one else noticed the problem.- John CommSec appears to be down btw!- LachlanFri 30 Oct 2026 at 11:14amFri 30 Oct 2026 at 11:14amHow Google counts its AI usersBy Katie SilverI noticed in Googles result that they are claiming 1 billion (?) users of Gemini. Is there any further detail on how they came to that number? Are they counting Gmail/google related accounts? Because while I have a google account via Gmail, I don't use Gemini unless google forces through search results. - allanYou'll be pleased to know, Allan, you're not counted. According to Google's official announcement and tech reports, the 1 billion monthly active user (MAU) milestone tracks individuals who deliberately open the dedicated Gemini app or go to google.com to type a prompt, use voice features or launch Gemini Live.Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 11:05amFri 30 Oct 2026 at 11:05amAnthropic IPO: Yay or nay?!By Katie SilverMorningstar's Lochlan Halloway writes that Anthropic's IPO could "be the biggest float ever, surpassing the record SpaceX set in June"."Most of us know Anthropic through its Claude model, or perhaps through the software bloodbath it set off in February this year. Claude proved it could write plausible-looking software in minutes, at a fraction of the cost and with a fraction of the expertise, and the 'SaaSpocalypse' ensued. The Australian tech index is still about a third below its August 2025 peak, and the US software applications index about a fifth below its own. It was such a fundamental challenge to the software business model that we rethought moats across our technology coverage, and of the 132 companies we reviewed, we downgraded the moat rating on 40," he said.The question is — is it overvalued? Halloway says at its proposed valuation it "would be worth almost as much as everything listed on the ASX put together". Not bad when you consider it was only founded in 2021, with Claude launching in 2023."But look at what Anthropic has done in that time. It went from $US1 billion of annual revenue to $US10 billion in about a year. Across nearly two decades of SEC filings, the only companies I could find that made the same leap as quickly were the Covid vaccine makers. By comparison, Google took three years to go from $US1 billion to $US10 billion, and Facebook four."Staggering figures but dare I mention the b-word? (*insert bubble emoji*). And can this kind of profit and growth continue?How much can the company keep making?According to Halloway, NYU professor Aswath Damodaran "puts the ceiling at the world's total wage bill, about $US26 trillion a year" while Anthropic is even more generous with itself, estimating $US40 trillion a year ("the work done by knowledge workers") … One wonders if they've used AI …But even if there is plenty of room to grow, will Claude be the model that wins? OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta and SpaceX are all chasing the same customers, and we don't know how this market shakes out.The next question, Holloway asks, is who makes the money? Is it Anthropic or its suppliers, like cloud computing companies (e.g. Amazon or Google) or chip-makers (e.g. Nvidia and TSMC).Airlines show how that can play out. They are the ones selling to us, but what they sell is close to a commodity, and they earn the lowest returns in the aviation supply chain. The suppliers with few rivals, such as the engine and parts makers and the booking systems, earn far more. As Richard Branson once quipped, the fastest way to become a millionaire is to start out as a billionaire, and go into the airline industry.The question is — can you lock customers in so a new agent isn't just a browser tab away? I'm thinking Apple here, which prioritises keeping everything in its ecosystem and makes it hard to switch between. As someone who keeps it casual with my AI agents, it's evident this will be a big challenge for Anthropic. Not least because you can ask ChatGPT, for example, to create an exportable file of everything it knows about you and then give it to another search engine. I typically do this monthly and then share the data around with my various agents.Halloway has some ideas for how Anthropic, or OpenAI, could create a "moat" that would protect against this and encourage loyalty/give the model a differential:"The first is a kind of network effect, in which the product gets better the more it is used. The more people use Claude to write code, the more Anthropic learns about what works. That makes its models and tools better, which brings in more users, who teach it more again."Fri 30 Oct 2026 at 10:44amFri 30 Oct 2026 at 10:44amH&M fined over flammable pyjamasBy Katie SilverH&M has paid $138,600 in penalties for allegedly selling more than 4,000 items of children's clothing that didn't adequately label fire warnings, according to the ACCC.The commission issued the clothing retailer with seven infringement notices for the alleged breaches of the Australian Consumer Law.The standard requires children's nightwear to carry an appropriate fire hazard label — either "high fire danger" or "low fire danger" depending on the composition of the garment and its flammability test results, according to the ACCC's statement.The images of the recalled clothing items are available here.Some of the pyjamas the ACCC alleges weren't given adequate flammable label warnings.
